document_check.note: Opwonya J, Ku B, Lee KH, Kim JI, Kim JU (2023) 'Eye movement changes as an indicator of mild cognitive impairment', Front. Neurosci. 17:1171417. It is a cross-sectional machine-learning classification study of 594 participants (428 CN, 166 MCI) from the GARD centre. The cited AUROC of 0.840 for demographics + MMSE + eye movements is reported (p1, p6).

cited_result: Discrimination of MCI from cognitively normal controls by the combined demographics + MMSE + eye-movement classifier: test-set AUROC 0.840 (XGB), compared with 0.767 for demographics + MMSE (LR).
tool_reason: The cited result is the discrimination (AUROC) of a multivariable machine-learning classifier for MCI diagnosis, so PROBAST applies, with the PROBAST+AI considerations.

domains.rationale: The sample is two diagnostic groups from a research dementia centre. The controls are called age-matched, but the groups differ in age. Exclusions (MRI lacunes or WMH grade 2 or more, visual impairment, AD dementia) take out cases that are harder to classify, compared with the primary-care screening use the authors intend.

signalling.question: 1.1 Were appropriate data sources used (e.g. cohort, RCT, or consecutive cross-sectional sample for a diagnostic model)?
signalling.quote: We divided the participants into MCI patient and age-matched CN control groups. MCI patients and CN controls were recruited at the Gwangju Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementia (GARD) center (Gwangju City, South Korea)

signalling.question: 1.1 (supplementary) Were the groups comparable as the 'age-matched' description implies?
signalling.quote: Patients with MCI were significantly older (p < 0.001) and had significantly lower MMSE total scores (p < 0.001) than CN controls.

signalling.question: 1.2 Were all inclusions and exclusions of participants appropriate?
signalling.quote: Exclusion criteria for the study were as follows: the presence of focal brain lesions on MRI, including lacunes and white matter hyperintensity lesions of grade 2 or more

domains.rationale: Eye-movement metrics come from one standardised device and pipeline, using rule-based response definitions applied to everyone. Demographics and MMSE would be available at the time of intended use.

signalling.question: 2.1 Were predictors defined and assessed in a similar way for all participants?
signalling.quote: We recorded SEM data on the Tobii Pro spectrum system (Tobii Pro AB, Danderyd, Sweden), sampled at 300 Hz, and processed with Tobii Pro Lab version 1.118.

signalling.question: 2.2 Were predictor assessments made without knowledge of outcome data?
signalling.quote: The standardized pipeline used to preprocess the gaze data collected for each participant has been described in detail elsewhere (Opwonya et al., 2022).

signalling.question: 2.3 Are all predictors available at the time the model is intended to be used?
signalling.quote: Brief cognitive measures, such as the MMSE that can be easily administered with minimal training are optimal for fast-paced, high-patient-volume screening settings

domains.rationale: The MCI reference diagnosis uses standard clinical criteria (CDR, SNSB-II, Albert et al.). However, the MMSE, which is a predictor in the cited model, was part of the SNSB-II battery the diagnosing clinicians used, so predictor information was built into the outcome. The interval between eye tracking and diagnosis is not reported.

signalling.question: 3.1 Was the outcome determined appropriately?
signalling.quote: CN controls were identified clinically as those who had a CDR score of zero and no sign of cognitive impairment; those with a CDR score of 0.5 and evidence of cognitive decline in one or more domains were considered MCI (Albert et al., 2011).

signalling.question: 3.2 Was a pre-specified or standard outcome definition used?
signalling.quote: MCI patients had a Seoul Neuropsychological Screening Battery-Second Edition (SNSB-II) z score of less than −1.5 in at least one of the domains.

signalling.question: 3.3 Were predictors excluded from the outcome definition?
signalling.quote: In our study, all participants were assessed using the Korean version of the MMSE, which was included in the SNSB-II (Park, 1989).

signalling.question: 3.4 Was the outcome defined and determined in a similar way for all participants?
signalling.quote: We examined all the participants through detailed clinical consultations, incorporating a neuropsychological battery and the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scale.

signalling.question: 3.5 Was the outcome determined without knowledge of predictor information?
signalling.quote: In our study, all participants were assessed using the Korean version of the MMSE, which was included in the SNSB-II (Park, 1989). [Searched for 'blind', 'masked', 'unaware': no statement on whether diagnosing clinicians were blind to eye-movement results.]

signalling.question: 3.6 Was the time interval between predictor assessment and outcome determination appropriate?
signalling.quote: Searched for the interval between the eye-tracking session and the clinical/neuropsychological assessment ('interval', 'same day', 'within'); only the enrolment window is given: 'In total, 679 individuals participated in the study between October 2019 and December 2020.'

domains.rationale: There are few events for the number of candidate predictors (about 133 MCI in training against about 34 candidates; about 33 MCI in the test set). Calibration is not assessed. Missing data are not reported, and participants who failed calibration are excluded. The reported 0.840 is the best of four algorithms on a single random test split, with no confidence interval and no external validation. Scaling appears to have been applied before the split. SMOTE and hyperparameter tuning were confined to training-set cross-validation.

signalling.question: 4.1 Were there a reasonable number of participants with the outcome?
signalling.quote: A total of 594 participants were included in the final analysis, including 428 CN controls and 166 MCI patients ... We randomly split the data into 80/20 train/test splits

signalling.question: 4.2 Were continuous and categorical predictors handled appropriately?
signalling.quote: We preprocessed all six datasets by mapping categorical features to binary variables, centering and scaling the continuous features, and removing features present in only one sample or all but one sample.

signalling.question: 4.3 Were all enrolled participants included in the analysis?
signalling.quote: and those who failed calibration and the preliminary trials that were conducted to familiarize participants with the task requirements before the actual trial

signalling.question: 4.4 Were participants with missing data handled appropriately?
signalling.quote: Searched for 'missing', 'imputation', 'incomplete': no statement on missing eye-movement, MMSE or demographic values.

signalling.question: 4.5 Was selection of predictors based on univariable analysis avoided?
signalling.quote: We studied the relationship between cognitive status and six feature sets

signalling.question: 4.6 Were complexities in the data (e.g. class imbalance) accounted for appropriately?
signalling.quote: Given that the data were imbalanced, we applied the synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) during cross-validation

signalling.question: 4.7 Were relevant model performance measures evaluated appropriately (discrimination and calibration)?
signalling.quote: Model performance was evaluated based on the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC).

signalling.question: 4.8 Were model overfitting, underfitting and optimism in model performance accounted for?
signalling.quote: We selected the optimal model based on the highest AUROC and lowest binomial deviance in each combination of learning algorithms and six feature sets. Subsequently, we evaluated the predictive performance of this model on the test set.

signalling.question: 4.9 Do predictors and their assigned weights in the final model correspond to the results from the reported multivariable analysis?
signalling.quote: No final model coefficients or tuned model are reported; only permutation importance: 'Feature importance was calculated using a permutation test'

signalling.question: AI: Is the train/test split at participant level (no person's data on both sides)?
signalling.quote: We randomly split the data into 80/20 train/test splits, and the train/test splits were identical across models generated with different feature sets for a valid comparison.

signalling.question: AI: Were preprocessing, oversampling and tuning confined to training folds?
signalling.quote: We preprocessed all six datasets by mapping categorical features to binary variables, centering and scaling the continuous features [scaling described on whole datasets]; Hyperparameters were selected via cross-validation on the training set to maximize the average area under the receiver operating characteristics curve (AUROC) across cross-validation folds.

signalling.question: AI: Was the test set held out from all tuning and model selection?
signalling.quote: Values in bold in each column represent the highest performance.

signalling.question: AI: Is reported performance apparent, internally validated, or externally validated?
signalling.quote: Specifically, we developed and validated prediction models with the ability to identify individuals with MCI using an ET paradigm comprising PS/AS and Go/No-go tasks [searched 'external': no external validation]

applicability.rationale: The authors intend primary-care screening. The sample is a research-centre two-group sample that excludes vascular MRI lesions, visual impairment and calibration failures.
Demographics, MMSE and a standard eye-tracking protocol are what would be used in practice.
MCI is defined by standard clinical criteria (CDR 0.5, SNSB-II, Albert et al. 2011).

overall_rationale: Three domains are high. Participants: a two-group research sample with exclusions that make classification easier. Outcome: the MMSE, a model predictor, was part of the diagnostic battery. Analysis: few events per candidate predictor, no calibration, the best of four algorithms reported from a single test split, calibration failures excluded, and no external validation. Under PROBAST, any high domain makes the overall rating high.
